The runout then continues down the Moose Creek Gully at a 20-30 degree angle down to 13,200' where the pitch steepens lower in the gully.","Leading up to the day of the avalanche, our party had discussed options for skiing, and decided to ski the Moose Creek Bowl of Mt Bross based on a video from the week prior which showed exceptional coverage for October. With the week of warm and wet weather before, we discussed that the snow underneath would likely be a firm melt freeze crust. On Saturday, it was forecasted to snow 5-10cm of snow on Mt Bross with moderate winds. We discussed that the new wind drifted snow overlying the firm crust would provide for possibly good skiing, but avalanche hazard was not discussed. Upon arrival to the trailhead on Sunday morning, we found ~10cm of new snow, and we were stoked about the prospect of good skiing. We also observed multiple other groups who had the same idea and were headed in the direction of Moose Creek Bowl. We quickly skinned up the Dolly Varden road before traversing to look at Moose Creek Bowl. It had great coverage, but we noticed the top 100 feet of the bowl looked smooth and pillowed, with wind drifted snow that looked like it might host a small but reactive wind slab. We discussed the possibility of an avalanche and agreed that it would most likely be isolated, and probably D1 in size; something relatively harmless to a skier. We continued up the east ridge, setting a skin track with two other groups of two closely behind. The spatial variability was large here, and surface conditions ranged from pencil hard old snow, to a dense wind drifted slab up to 20 cm thick. We noticed moderate cracking and collapsing, and figured there was probably some weak snow resting on the rocks below that caused those places with deeper wind drifted snow to collapse. Skier 3 dug a quick hand pit, and found the wind drifted snow to shear on the crust below, but we determined that this slab was isolated and unlikely to propagate across the entire slope. As we continued up the ridge, we watched a party of 3 ski the lookers right side of the bowl. The top looked like firm wind drifted snow but it looked to quickly soften into good powder 100' down. We were stoked. 
As we reached the top of the bowl, we hurried our transition with the intention of skiing the bowl before the other groups behind us. We decided on skiing the center of the bowl. Skiers 2 and 3 both felt nervous about skiing this slope, but didn't say anything because the snow cover is so thin, an avalanche seemed unlikely, and the rest of the group seemed stoked. Skier 1 felt that there was potential for a slide as well, but thought that it would be a small isolated wind slab, D1 in size that would easily be managed on skis.
Skier 3 suggested that Skier 1 perform a ski cut to mitigate the hazard safely, but Skier 1 didn't want to do that and communicated that they were going to ski it fast down the center.
The group completed a beacon check before leaving the top, and Skier 1 promptly skied down the slope, noticing no signs of instability and stopping on the mining road in the center of the path 500 feet down. Skier 1 noticed that the wind drifted snow near the top of the starting zone was supportable to skis and hollow sounding, but quickly transitioned to softer, shallower new snow. Skier 1 did not communicate this to Skiers 2 and 3.
